title: Your Brain Edits Real Memories: Why 25% Recalled a Fake Day
description:
Documentary case briefing on How Elizabeth Loftus Planted a Lost-in-the-Mall Memory in 25% of Adults, grounded in ['Elizabeth F Loftus' (1995) (Psychiatric Annals). Empirical findings show that in 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed 45 students films of two cars colliding and changed one verb: 'smashed' yielded 40.8 mph estimates versus 31.8 mph for 'contacted'.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how hippocampus, temporal lobe, prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that one week later, 32 percent of the 'smashed' group swore they saw broken glass on the road compared with 14 percent of the 'hit' group, even though zero broken glass existed in the film.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- ['Elizabeth F Loftus', 'Jacqueline E Pickrell'] (1995). The Formation of False Memories. Psychiatric Annals. https://doi.org/10.3928/0048-5713-19951201-07
- ['Elizabeth F. Loftus', 'John C. Palmer'] (1974). Reconstruction of automobile destruction: An example of the interaction between language and memory. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(74)80011-3
- ['Martin J. Chadwick', 'Raeesa S. Anjum', 'Dharshan Kumaran', 'Daniel L. Schacter', 'Hugo J. Spiers', 'Demis Hassabis'] (2016). Semantic representations in the temporal pole predict false memories. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1610686113
